source.title: VASSO: Variance Suppression for Sharpness-Aware Minimization
source.authors: Bing-Cong Li; Yilang Zhang; G. B. Giannakis

record.tranche_reason: The study compares training methods and measures test performance and Hessian-based flatness, but does not reproduce the specific interventions or measurements in the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports VASSO, SAM, and other optimizer results on generalization, plus Hessian-spectrum measurements. It does not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected networks, the listed adaptive-optimizer or batch-size claims, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Cited prior-work results are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses the premise that flatter minima improve generalization to develop VASSO and evaluates its performance. None of its own results tests V1–V8. In particular, Hessian eigenvalues and loss-landscape plots do not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its ranking of train–test gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that variance suppression provably stabilizes SAM's stochastic linearization and improves empirical generalization across vision and language tasks; eVASSO improves the generalization–computation tradeoff. These are the authors' conclusions, not tests of the listed claim versions.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes an EMA-based variance-suppression method for SAM and evaluates its test performance; it does not use the claim versions’ interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary by model, dataset, task, noise level, and VASSO hyperparameter θ; eVASSO outcomes also vary with computation probability p.

fits_no_version.finding: VASSO generally improves held-out performance over SAM across vision and translation tasks. Table 8 reports lower largest Hessian eigenvalue and eigenvalue ratio for VASSO than SAM, but does not report magnitude-aware sharpness or train–test gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Variance suppression in SAM can improve held-out performance and reduce Hessian-based sharpness in the tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 2(c) varies the subsample used to construct SAM's adversary, with smaller subsamples worsening translation BLEU. This does not compare large and small parameter-update batches as V5 requires.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reducing the adversary-construction subsample size can worsen SAM's translation performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 5 compares SAM and VASSO with 25%, 50%, and 75% corrupted training labels, reporting test accuracy without random-label training fit or a fully randomized-label condition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Variance suppression can improve SAM's robustness to partial training-label corruption.

record.problems: Some comparisons reuse results from prior work, including SAM and GSAM results for DomainBed. ImageNet ResNet-50 results average only 2 independent runs. The paper reports test accuracy and related metrics, not train-test gaps for its own proposed method.
record.rows_left_out: No rows: the results concern VASSO and Hessian-spectrum measures, which do not measure the specific behaviors or magnitude-aware sharpness named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels alongside natural-label generalization using the same architecture and recipe; chance-level held-out accuracy for random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning, including broader tuning and recovery recipes.
Large versus small update batches under fixed epoch budgets and recipes that reduce any penalty.
Effects of adding or removing dropout and its interactions with dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with train–test gaps at similarly low training loss, and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The empty row set is appropriate for V1–V8. ASAM and FisherSAM comparisons concern adaptive perturbations within SAM, rather than the adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison in V4. Adam and AdamW serve as base optimizers; the study provides no controlled comparison with SGD on the same workload.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy on natural versus random labels.
Width sweeps beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under the stated tuning conditions and recovery recipes.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and adaptive recipes.
Dropout addition, removal, and interaction with training-set size or data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbation tolerance, comparison with norm- and margin-based measures, and its ranking of train-test gaps.
Removing memorized examples and comparing the resulting test accuracy with random-example removal.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
